title: Will the Immigration and Asylum Bill protect survivors of modern slavery?
label: 11 November 2026 · Modern slavery protections
summary: The committee questioned three experts about changes to how the Bill would identify and support victims of modern slavery. The witnesses said the current system has serious weaknesses, but argued that the Bill would make it harder for victims to be believed, receive support and remain in the UK while recovering. They welcomed some measures for children, while calling for stronger safeguards, continued support after age 18 and decisions based on children’s best interests.

speakers.label: Eleonora Fais
speakers.name: Eleonora Fais
speakers.role: Anti-Trafficking Monitoring Group Coordinator, Anti-Slavery International

glossary.definition: The UK system for referring people who may have been trafficked or enslaved so authorities can decide whether they are victims and what support they need.
An early decision on whether there are reasonable grounds to believe someone may be a victim of modern slavery.
The later decision on whether someone is confirmed to be a victim of modern slavery.
The Council of Europe convention that sets requirements for preventing human trafficking and protecting its victims.
The European Convention on Human Rights, an agreement that protects basic rights and freedoms.
A period of at least 30 days intended to let a possible trafficking victim recover and consider their options.
A rule that can exclude some people from protection as trafficking victims on public safety grounds.
A defence in law that may protect victims from conviction for some crimes they were forced to commit because of their exploitation.
Independent advocates who help children who may have been trafficked and make sure their needs are heard.

chapters.title: Problems with the current system
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses praised the number of victims identified but said weak referrals and poor decisions already make it difficult for survivors to get help.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Bill changes how victims of modern slavery are identified and supported. Does it fix problems in the current system?

turns.speaker: Eleanor Lyons
turns.text: The system identified more than 23,000 victims last year and offered them support. But first-contact organisations don't always know how to refer people, and referrals can be inconsistent or poorly prepared.

turns.speaker: Eleanor Lyons
turns.text: The Home Office has also been making weaker decisions about who is a victim, while the Government hasn't published a modern slavery strategy for a long time. Perpetrators aren't being prosecuted enough either. The Bill doesn't solve these problems.

turns.speaker: Professor Parosha Chandran
turns.text: The UK has built up laws and guidance over many years. But people who may have been trafficked still can't refer themselves to the national referral mechanism; they need a recognised organisation to do it, and many front-line workers lack specialist training.

turns.speaker: Professor Parosha Chandran
turns.text: People can be treated as immigration offenders, suspects or unreliable witnesses before anyone properly considers whether they've been exploited. More than a quarter of people accepted as trafficking victims are British nationals, so this isn't only an immigration issue.

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: Recent changes have made the system harder to access, based on claims of misuse that haven't been supported by evidence. Before the Nationality and Borders Act changes began in January 2023, nine in ten people received a positive early decision. By June 2026, it was 64%.

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: But 81% of the cases reconsidered later received a positive decision. That suggests the initial decisions are often failing people. The answer should be to improve identification and protection, not restrict access further.

chapters.title: Whether victims will be believed
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses argued that treating late, inconsistent or similar accounts as evidence against victims could deter them from seeking help and breach the UK's obligations.

turns.speaker: Baroness Maclean of Redditch
turns.text: The Bill says delays, inconsistencies, missing details and strikingly similar accounts should count against a person's credibility. Is that compatible with the UK's duties to identify and protect victims?

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: We believe it isn't. The law requires a system that can identify and protect victims in practice. This clause risks turning common signs of exploitation into reasons to disbelieve someone.

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: Traffickers tell people they won't be believed, will be punished or deported, and won't get help. Putting those doubts into law could reinforce the threats and stop victims coming forward.

turns.speaker: Eleanor Lyons
turns.text: Survivors may not remember the order of events, especially after trauma, or may describe experiences similar to other victims'. Making those things grounds for disbelief would send a damaging message: if you come forward, you won't be believed.

turns.speaker: Professor Parosha Chandran
turns.text: Courts and prosecutors have recognised that victims may disclose late or give incomplete or inconsistent accounts because of trauma, threats or instructions from traffickers. The authorities shouldn't accept that when prosecuting offenders but reject it when deciding whether victims deserve protection.

turns.speaker: Professor Parosha Chandran
turns.text: Similar accounts can happen when people are controlled in the same way or exploited by the same group. In cases of child sexual exploitation, authorities have wrongly dismissed children whose accounts were delayed or messy, only to find later that their accounts were similar.

turns.speaker: Professor Parosha Chandran
turns.text: The European Court of Human Rights has also said people shouldn't have to identify themselves as trafficking victims. Once there's a credible suspicion, officials should make enquiries and allow time for the person to explain what happened.

chapters.title: Support, disqualification and criminalisation
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses warned that ending support after a negative decision or excluding victims too readily could leave them exposed to homelessness, removal and further exploitation.

turns.speaker: Baroness Maclean of Redditch
turns.text: The Bill could end the 30-day recovery and reflection period as soon as a person is told they're not a victim. What would that mean?

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: The 30 days are meant to give people time to recover, understand the process and begin getting help. If officials decide too quickly, victims may be asked for detailed evidence before they've even met a support worker.

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: A person who gets a negative decision may lose support and become homeless or destitute, leaving them open to further exploitation. They may also be at risk of removal and unable to get their case reconsidered.

turns.speaker: Professor Parosha Chandran
turns.text: I believe ending the period early is incompatible with the UK's human rights duties. In cases I've taken to the European Court, people wrongly identified as not trafficked faced losing specialist care and shelter. One woman had gone without trauma-related care for ten years.

turns.speaker: Eleanor Lyons
turns.text: Poor decisions already push people out of support, only for the decision later to be overturned. That cycle can expose them to survival sex, re-trafficking and further exploitation. The surrounding system isn't strong enough to justify cutting support sooner.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: What about excluding victims from protection on national security, public order or bad-faith grounds, and protecting them from punishment for crimes caused by their exploitation?

turns.speaker: Eleanor Lyons
turns.text: These exclusions should be exceptional, not used as a blanket rule. It's welcome that children have been removed from the general public order exclusion. We also need to know whether the legal defence for victims forced to commit crimes is actually being used.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: Lawyers representing defendants don't always seem to know about that defence. Do we know how often it's used?

turns.speaker: Eleanor Lyons
turns.text: No. I've heard opposing claims: some say it's used too little, others that it's misused. We should ask law enforcement how it's applied before bringing in measures that could exclude more exploited people.

turns.speaker: Professor Parosha Chandran
turns.text: A recent High Court judgment said the authorities had failed to assess the risk of someone being trafficked again by other people. The Bill could let the Government stop the victim-identification process before that assessment is completed.

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: The public order exclusion has disproportionately affected people exploited in crime: 58% of those excluded on that ground had experienced criminal exploitation. The separate bad-faith exclusion could prevent officials from making even an initial decision about whether someone may be a victim.

turns.speaker: Lord Murray of Blidworth
turns.text: Surely the Home Secretary should be able to limit protection where there are genuine national security or public order concerns?

turns.speaker: Eleanor Lyons
turns.text: Yes, if the power is used exceptionally. The concern is using it as a one-size-fits-all rule. And although children are exempt from the general public order exclusion, they can still be excluded on national security grounds.

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: That shouldn't apply to children. They can't consent to being exploited or choose to enter the referral system.

chapters.title: Leave to remain and recovery
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses said most survivors granted permission to stay do so because they need time to recover, and alternative immigration routes aren't guaranteed.

turns.speaker: Euan Stainbank
turns.text: The Bill limits when the Government must give victims temporary permission to stay so they can recover. What would that change mean?

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: Figures shared by the Helen Bamber Foundation show that 524 survivors were granted permission to stay for recovery in 2025. That was 92% of all grants to survivors that year.

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: Without that permission, people may struggle to rebuild their lives and could be removed from the UK. People with insecure immigration status are more vulnerable to homelessness, unable to access services, and easier targets for traffickers.

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: We can't assume they can use another route, such as asylum. Not everyone qualifies, and even those who apply aren't guaranteed permission to stay.

turns.speaker: Professor Parosha Chandran
turns.text: The law introduced in 2022 recognised that confirmed victims may need permission to stay to recover. I haven't seen an explanation in the Bill's published material for why that reasoning has changed.

turns.speaker: Euan Stainbank
turns.text: Could the 92% have qualified instead because they needed to help the authorities or claim compensation?

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: They might have qualified on those grounds, but they weren't granted permission that way. They were granted it because they needed time to recover.

chapters.title: When support can be withdrawn
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses warned that support rules may punish people for difficulties caused by trauma or by problems with housing and other services.

turns.speaker: Baroness Chakrabarti
turns.text: The Bill could remove support during the recovery period in some situations. When might victims lose help, and would that meet the UK's obligations?

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: We believe the change conflicts with the duty to support survivors. People may fail to meet service rules because of trauma, because they don't understand the system, or because of problems with asylum accommodation or local-authority housing.

turns.speaker: Baroness Chakrabarti
turns.text: So someone could lose help for reasons outside their control, including failures or rules in housing and other services?

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: Yes. For example, someone might leave housing because of trauma or other pressures, and then become unable to get support through the modern slavery service.

turns.speaker: Professor Parosha Chandran
turns.text: The Bill may require officials to prove that a person's difficulty was caused specifically by the trafficking. But people can have overlapping needs, such as a disability, mental illness or earlier exploitation. It could be impossible to separate those causes fairly.

turns.speaker: Eleanor Lyons
turns.text: If you take away care and shelter, people may end up sleeping rough and exposed to exploitation. The change may also apply differently in England and Wales than in Scotland and Northern Ireland, creating different levels of support across the UK.

turns.speaker: Baroness Chakrabarti
turns.text: Could that difference between the nations raise further human rights concerns?

turns.speaker: Professor Parosha Chandran
turns.text: It could. The human rights convention also prohibits certain kinds of discrimination. Different treatment across the UK might be unlawful if it goes along with a breach of another protected right.

chapters.title: Safeguards for children
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses welcomed stronger advocacy for children but called for protection beyond age 18, no credibility tests for children and decisions centred on their best interests.

turns.speaker: Afzal Khan
turns.text: Does the Bill protect child victims' best interests? What else is needed?

turns.speaker: Eleanor Lyons
turns.text: It's good that independent child trafficking guardians will be written into law. They help wrap support around exploited children. Local safeguarding teams also need to work together on long-term care.

turns.speaker: Eleanor Lyons
turns.text: Support shouldn't suddenly end at 18. Young people who have been in care need continued help as they move into adulthood. Children also shouldn't have to meet the Bill's new tests for credibility.

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: I welcome the wider guardian service, but it doesn't cover the difficult transition after someone turns 18. Children's credibility shouldn't be questioned, and the public order exclusion shouldn't apply to them on any grounds.

turns.speaker: Eleonora Fais
turns.text: Children should be given permission to stay based on their best interests. That should be the main test, rather than relying on the other routes available to adults.

turns.speaker: Professor Parosha Chandran
turns.text: A child doesn't need to have faced force or threats to be trafficked. Children are vulnerable because of their age; they may not know they're being exploited and may be unable to explain what has happened.

turns.speaker: Professor Parosha Chandran
turns.text: The Bill doesn't put the child's best interests clearly into the law itself. Each part that affects children should be checked for its impact. Overall, I believe the changes would be a serious step backwards for victims in the UK and internationally.
